@@117909207 <p> Whoever decided to hold the G20 summit in Rio de Janeiro at the same time as the UN COP29 climate conference in Baku clearly had a sense of humour . Would heads of state meeting in Brazil this week agree to the same things as their environment ministers meeting 12,000 kilometres away in Azerbaijan ? <p> It turns out that the answer -- comically or tragically , according to taste -- is no . The big advance at last year 's COP28 was that countries committed to " transitioning away from fossil fuels " . <p> After more than a quarter of a century of climate talks , this was a real breakthrough : so much so that the UN 's official press release hailed the agreement as " the beginning of the end of the fossil fuel era " . <p> At this week 's G20 summit , you would never have known that happened . The climate change section of the 22-page Rio communique repeats various COP28 commitments -- a trebling of renewable energy , for instance -- but not the commitment to transition away from fossil @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and Saudi Arabia refused . In the end , the others had to be content with a general endorsement of the COP28 agreement as a whole . <p> How can this happen ? How can countries agree to something in one multilateral forum and reject it in another ? The answer tells us something about how climate change has become a contested arena of global governance . <p> Russia and Saudi Arabia make up one-tenth of the G20 's membership . In a decision-making process requiring unanimity , they can block agreement . In the nearly-200-strong UN Framework Convention on Climate Change , though , they and the other recalcitrant petrostates make up around one-fiftieth of the membership , and they can more easily be defeated by the other 98% , which is exactly what happened at last year 's COP . <p> What makes this interesting is that it represents two opposing visions of how the world should make decisions about " global public goods " . These are things , such as a safe climate , from which all the world 's people benefit , and they can @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The protection of the oceans and biodiversity are other critical environmental examples . ) <p> On the one side is the vision underpinning the G20 . The world 's largest economies should make the decisions about climate because they are responsible for over 80% of the world 's greenhouse gas emissions . <p> It is what they do that really matters . Since all the big countries are anxious not to be outcompeted by the others , only if all of them agree to act will each feel able to do so . If excluding smaller countries looks unfair , well that 's just realpolitik . <p> On the other side is the vision underpinning the UN . Climate change affects all countries , so all of them should make the decisions together . It has a particularly severe impact on the least-developed countries and small island states , which are most vulnerable to climate change yet have done least to cause it . <p> That is fundamentally a question of justice , which makes it imperative that smaller countries are part of the decision-making process . <p> As climate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is coming to a head . As COP29 here in Baku is proving once again , the UNFCCC is a desperately unwieldy body . Encompassing so many different countries with such vastly different circumstances and national interests , its negotiations can be tortuous . <p> Some of the complexity is removed by organising the countries into groups , but then recomplicated by some countries belonging to more than one group . ( Many African nations belong simultaneously to the Africa group , the Least Developed Countries group and the overarching " G77 and China " group . ) <p> A bewildering array of technical processes on different aspects of climate action is further complicated by overlapping mandates . The language in which they are expressed is painfully jargon-ridden , making it largely incomprehensible to the journalists who follow it , let alone to a layperson . <p> As a result , the annual COPs , or " conferences of the parties " , have become theatrical combat zones in which previous agreements are frequently challenged and battles refought , culminating every year in a tense " endgame " stand-off in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ in a last-minute deal long after the conference is meant to have ended . <p> And beyond the negotiating rooms the COPs have got larger and larger , as the entire global " climate community " -- businesses , investors , NGOs , academics , lobbyists and media -- comes to town to network with one another , do deals and promote themselves . Around 65,000 people registered for Baku 's COP ; last year , in the more attractive location of Dubai , it was almost 100,000 . <p> It is no wonder that many people are walking away from the circus . This year they were joined by some of the UN 's own luminaries . In an open letter published on the eve of the conference , former UN secretary-general Ban Ki-Moon , former UNFCCC executive secretary Christiana Figueres and other leading climate figures called for reform of the whole COP process . No longer should countries not committed to the transition from fossil fuels be allowed to host the negotiations , they said . ( All of the last four hosts have been oil-producing states . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of commitments , not more on rulemaking , with proper accountability for country pledges and tracking of promised finance . The involvement of businesses -- particularly fossil fuel companies -- should be reduced , with scientists given more prominence . <h> What is a ' developing ' country ? <p> Some of these things are conceivable ; others ( such as the choice of hosts ) almost certainly not . But another suggested reform is actually one of the critical topics of the Baku negotiations . This is the question of whether Saudi Arabia and other rich oil states , along with China , should continue to be counted as " developing countries " . <p> Under the UNFCCC rules , they still are . The original UN treaty was signed in 1992 , when the world was divided fairly obviously into the industrialised " developed " countries ( Europe , North America , Japan , Australia and New Zealand ) and everyone else . ( Oddly , Turkey was also counted as " developed " , a categorisation it has been contesting ever since . ) <p> Back then @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ US$1,000 . It is now around $25,000 . Saudi Arabia 's is now over $55,000 , and the United Arab Emirates nearly $85,000 . ( The US figure is $82,000 , Australia 's $66,000 . ) <p> Meanwhile , China has become the world 's largest producer of greenhouse gases -- overtaking the European Union , it was revealed this week , in cumulative historic emissions . <p> In these circumstances , the developed countries argue , the binary division of the UN climate regime into " developed " and " developing " countries has outlived its usefulness . <p> The Paris climate agreement , signed in 2015 , partially acknowledged this . As recounted by former US climate envoy Todd Stern in a candid new book about how the agreement was reached , breaching the binary division involved many years of difficult negotiations . But in the end , it was agreed that the responsibility to produce a national emissions reduction plan should be an equal obligation on all countries , irrespective of income . <p> What could not be agreed in Paris , however , was that the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ climate change should also extend beyond the developed world . Instead , that responsibility remained firmly with the advanced economies whose historic emissions were the cause of the climate crisis . <p> When the Paris Agreement reiterated that $100 billion in climate finance should flow to poorer countries each year ( a figure first agreed in 2009 -- 10 ) , the obligation remained very much rooted in the binary division of nations . <p> That is being contested in Baku . The Paris Agreement set an end date of 2025 for the $100 billion commitment , so COP29 is negotiating a new financial objective , elegantly called the " New Collective Quantified Goal " , or NCQG . Its price tag is one focus of the negotiations ; the other is who should pay it . <p> For the developed countries , the answer is clear : they are happy to continue paying but only if the obligation is widened to include Saudi Arabia , the UAE , other rich oil states and China . The criterion should be the ability to pay , or " fair shares " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> They point to a telling precedent . At this week 's G20 summit , South Korea announced a significant pledge to the World Bank 's fund for the world 's poorest countries , the International Development Association . Korea was once one of IDA 's recipient countries . But as it has grown rich enough over the past 30 years to " graduate " into the donor category . The developed countries argue the same principle should apply within the climate regime . <p> The Saudis and China reject this out of hand . This is not because they do n't provide assistance to poorer countries . On the contrary , speaking in Baku last week Chinese vice-premier Ding Xuexiang pointedly declared that , since 2016 , China has " provided and mobilised " approximately US$24 billion to support other developing countries in addressing climate change . As others noted , this would make it the fifth- or sixth-largest provider of climate finance after Japan , Germany , the United States , France and Britain . <p> China 's announcement was telling . <p> On the one hand @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ would see China stepping into the breach to claim a global leadership role on climate change . On the other , its language precisely mirrored the way the Paris Agreement defines the obligation of developed countries . <p> But China was absolutely unequivocal : as stipulated by the agreement , these were " voluntary contributions " . Only the developed countries had legal obligations to pay up . <h> A climate paradox ? <p> As the Baku negotiations reach their conclusion , it is n't clear how the impasse between developed and developing countries on who should pay will be resolved . Over in Rio de Janeiro , though , the developed countries , China and Saudi Arabia were reaching their own agreement on how it should be done . <p> Expertly marshalled by President Lula of Brazil , the G20 leaders committed to making the World Bank and the regional multilateral development banks , or MDBs , in Africa , Asia , Latin America and the Caribbean " bigger , better and more effective " . <p> Endorsing a detailed reform " roadmap " for the MDBs drawn up @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ accelerate the reform of the international financial architecture so that it can meet the urgent challenge of sustainable development , climate change and efforts to eradicate poverty " . This should include reform of the International Monetary Fund , action to support heavily indebted developing countries , and measures to help mobilise more money from the private sector . <p> Herein lies the paradox of the global climate regime . The UNFCCC insists it is the only legitimate body to agree on the climate finance goal . But it is only the G20 -- the major economic powers -- that can effectively decide how it happens . <p> Or perhaps it 's not a paradox , but simply a sensible division of labour between the two competing principles of justice and realpolitik .

@@117994707 <h> By insisting that Australia 's housing crisis is all about supply , governments are ignoring the decades-long trend of shrinking households , which is also contributing to social isolation . By Hugh Mackay . <h> An overlooked cause of the housing crisis <p> In a rare display of unanimity , politicians , economists , journalists and assorted commentators all seem to agree that the solution to the present housing crisis is to increase supply . There might be disagreements about what kind of housing , how much of it should be social housing , the desirable level of density , or where it should be built , but there 's widespread consensus on the urgent need to build more houses . <p> At the risk of sounding economically illiterate , I suspect the chief villain in the housing crisis is not supply , but an unsustainable shift in the pattern of demand . <p> Consider three salient facts about the Australian housing market . <p> First , our shrinking households . In the past 100 years , the Australian population has increased fivefold , while the number of households @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ been creating households at twice the rate we 've been growing the population . Over this period , the average Australian home has shrunk from about 4.5 to 2.5 occupants . <p> Today , more than 25 per cent of Australian households contain just one person . Single-person and two-person households between them account for well over half of all Australian households , and the former is now our fastest-growing type . <p> Second , our bloated houses . While our households have been shrinking , the size of our houses has more than doubled in the past 75 years . In 1950 , the average Australian house occupied about 100 square metres . Today , the average is about 250 square metres . <p> About 36 per cent of all Australian homes contain three bedrooms , and almost one third has four or more . Many , if not most , of our single- and two-person households occupy three-bedroom dwellings , so we have become a nation of spare rooms . <p> The third fact is that , on the night of the last census in 2021 , more @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ many plausible explanations for that : some occupiers were away on holiday on census night ; some of those empty houses were holiday homes not currently in use ; some were the " other " house of people wealthy enough to divide their time between two dwellings ; some were investment properties whose owners were content to watch the value increase without having the hassle of tenants . ( Imagine offering negative gearing as an incentive to multiple home ownership ! In France , you 'd be taxed for owning more than one dwelling . ) <p> Put those three factors together -- shrinking households , expanding house size and underused houses -- and it 's surely an oversimplification to say that Australia has a housing shortage . It would be more realistic to say we have been distributing the people among the houses in ways that promote waste ( overinvesting in bigger houses than we need ) , drive inequality ( multiple home ownership at the top of the heap ; an inability to buy into the market at the bottom ) and increase the risk of social isolation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ by the housing choices we 've been making over the past half-century in particular , we 've actually been driving a social trend that is bad for our mental health as individuals , and likely to erode social cohesion as well . <p> It 's strange that we have for so long been pursuing housing strategies that are bad for our economic and social health . <p> Why are we so enthusiastically opting for smaller -- especially single-person -- households ? It would be dangerous to generalise about this . Some solo householders have deliberately chosen to live alone as a symbol of their freedom and independence . They may say : " I have family , friends , work colleagues , neighbours -- I can socialise all I want , but I like nothing better than coming home , shutting the door behind me , punching the air and saying , ' Alone at last ! ' ? " <p> At the other end of a very broad spectrum of solo householders are those who ache with loneliness . Pitchforked into " singleton " status by bereavement , relationship @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ yearn for someone to share their space . They may turn the TV on before they leave the house so they wo n't feel as if they 're returning to an empty , silent space . <p> While it would be wrong to characterise all solo householders as lonely ( and of course , it 's possible to feel lonely in a marriage or a crowded house ) , the risk of widespread social isolation is greatly increased in a society where every fourth household contains just one person . <p> " We are not meant to live alone . " That was one of the most common remarks I heard from solo householders on the many occasions when , as a social researcher , I listened to their stories . They have a point . As members of an inherently social species , we need each other , and we run the risk of damaging our mental health when we spend too much time alone . <p> It 's no secret that our society is in the grip of epidemics of loneliness , anxiety and depression , and social @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ malaise . It 's also associated with a heightened risk of hypertension , inflammation , sleep disorders , vulnerability to addiction and even reduced life expectancy . <p> There are many contributors to social isolation -- not least , paradoxically , the excessive use of social media -- but solo households must be close to the top of the list . <p> As our households continue to shrink , we can assume that the incidence of social isolation will increase . So we need to recognise that , by the housing choices we 've been making over the past half-century in particular , we 've actually been driving a social trend that is bad for our mental health as individuals , and likely to erode social cohesion as well . <p> In some ways , the rot set in in the 1930s when the nuclear family -- mum , dad and their kids -- became fashionable as the household unit . There are good grounds to wonder whether that was a socially healthy trend -- for parents or children -- but that 's another story . What it has meant @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ shrinkage , and that " empty-nesters " has become a new and increasingly common household type . <p> There was a time when we thought of households quite differently : more complex , more fluid , often three-generational , with assorted aunts , uncles , grandparents or lodgers coming and going . <p> So what is the solution ? While there is some creative thinking about housing among urban planners , too many local councils are rushing to the conclusion that high-rise apartment blocks are the answer to the housing crisis . <p> My own research has consistently pointed to the conclusion that , given our contemporary patterns of living , medium-density housing is the most socially healthy way for us to live -- dense enough to promote the incidental social encounters that are the lifeblood of " the village " but not dense enough to encourage an obsession with security and privacy -- the common effect of packing too many people into too small a space . <p> Even the traditional suburban house and garden is no longer the " golden mean " . With our low birthrate , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and after-school care , such housing is less likely to promote a healthy neighbourliness than the medium-density options of terrace houses , townhouses and low-rise apartments . <p> The present high cost of housing could well be the catalyst for more creative , more flexible -- and socially healthier -- thinking about households , as a way of easing the demand for housing and thereby lowering house prices . Already , more adult offspring are living in the family home for longer , and many families are beginning to ponder the three-generational possibility . <p> Perhaps we need many more " granny flats " . We might even begin to reverse the trend towards either warehousing the elderly in institutional settings or leaving them to live alone -- as one third of women over 65 currently do . Knowing what we know about the health hazards of solo living , when did we decide that would be a good idea ? <p> Within my own circle , some people have been re-examining the lodger option -- perhaps taking in a student or two , or nurses from a nearby hospital @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to facilitate more of these arrangements . Others , especially close friends approaching retirement , are weighing up the pros and cons of shared housing . <p> The former governor of the Reserve Bank Philip Lowe once remarked that one solution to the housing crisis would be to increase the number of people per household . Though his remarks were widely criticised , he hit the nail on the head , economically speaking . " I 've been using these specific images , like of Grenfell Tower , of these complicated things that occur . And there are certain types of images that seem to be the most haunting of that moment that somehow stay with me or haunt me the most . And that 's the kind of image that I tend to work with . " <p> Mehretu blurs these images , which then become a foundation to which her work responds . The result is ambitious , energetic abstract paintings that can measure seven by 24 metres . They incorporate architectural drawings and maps , offering viewers different vantage points to experience the works . <p> This is what makes her work unique and distinct -- not just its scale , but the complexity of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . The deeply layered abstractions she produces invite viewers to make their own interpretations and make defining Mehretu 's work impossible . To do so would not only be reductive but a failure of the imagination . She invites viewers to find a new language in the ways we see the world . <p> " I prefer the space for opacity because I think there 's a lot more space for liberation there , where you 're not having to describe yourself or define yourself or present yourself , " she tells me . @@117994718 <h> Melbourne Theatre Company 's jubilant musical adaptation of Miles Franklin 's My Brilliant Career breathes new life and vibrancy into an Australian classic . By Keith Gow . <h> MTC 's My Brilliant Career is miles ahead <p> In the introduction to Miles Franklin 's 1901 debut , My Brilliant Career , the character of Sybylla Melvyn wants to set expectations . This is not a romance , she tells us . It 's not a novel , either . Just a yarn . " I have too often faced the music of life to the tune of hardship , " she says , " to waste time in ... fantasies and dreams . " This story is going to be real . <p> A new stage adaptation of this classic Australian work by Melbourne Theatre Company embraces this reference to the " music of life " to create a rambunctious musical for our times . As the audience enters , a band of musicians is already on stage , playing loudly and exuberantly . We 've just walked into live-music night at the local country pub . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the musical Once , staged at Melbourne 's Princess Theatre in 2014 , but instead of an Irish pub , it 's larrikin Aussies with a bush poet vibe . Its brash , lo-fi style also bears some similarity to the work coming out of the Hayes Theatre in Sydney -- Richard Carroll 's production of Calamity Jane , a jubilant modern take on that story . Fittingly , the co-artistic director of the Hayes , Victoria Falconer , is the musical director of My Brilliant Career . She 's present with the rest of the musicians , breathing new life and vibrancy into this classic work . <p> The band doubles as the acting ensemble , a multi-talented team of performers spinning the tale of a young girl and her ambitions . Actor Kala Gare steps out front , ready to take charge as emcee , lead singer and lead character Sybylla . She welcomes her " dear fellow Australians " to life on the farm . She 's 15 and dreams of a future in music , literature and theatre . But reality is bleak : drought has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ family 's subsistence living is monotonous . <p> The plot -- what there is of it -- does n't stray far from the original . Sybylla is shipped from her family home to her grandmother 's estate , because her parents ca n't afford to keep her and she might find a husband there . Sybylla wants none of that : her desire is to nurture her creative ambitions rather than tend to a garden or a man . <p> MTC 's My Brilliant Career embraces how far we 've come , knowing there 's still some way to go . It 's a joy to see an Australian musical that is fully formed in its first production . <p> As the members of the ensemble play multiple characters , they each get a chance to shine . Cameron Bajraktarevic-Hayward 's Frank is suitably stuck-up , and his song " Brick " , an attempt to woo Sybylla , is hilarious . Christina O'Neill wows as Aunt Helen -- her gorgeous voice entreats Sybylla to " Turn Away from the Mirror " , a song about looking beyond your flaws @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the matriarch of the rowdy M'Swat family . Raj Labade smoulders with charm as the love interest , Harry , serenading the girl of his dreams as she acts like the child she is . <p> But this hardworking group of actors is there to support the leading lady 's quest to find her voice . And what a voice it is . <p> Gare -- who was last seen on stage in Melbourne as Anne Boleyn in SIX the Musical , another musically contemporary period piece -- has tremendous range . Sybylla is selfish , arrogant and loud , but she also believes she is plain and may have nothing to say through her art . For every outburst of rage , Gare shows us Sybylla turning inward , trying to articulate her thoughts on life . Gare 's performance is spellbinding and Melbourne will be talking about it for a long time to come . <p> Olivier Award-winning designer Marg Horwell covers the stage with dried yellow grass , with a raised platform in the middle that features an upright piano . Throughout the show , Horwell overlays @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ parasols -- and in one vibrant scene , a curtain of multicoloured streamers -- as times and Sybylla 's circumstances change . Horwell 's costumes are striking , without feeling like stuffy period replicas . <p> If there were any concerns that this show might not rise above being an amusing reimagination of a classic , the song " In the Wrong Key " changes things up . It starts as a simple tune , Gare singing and accompanying herself on the piano , and then , one by one , the full band joins in . At the climax , Gare stands defiantly on top of the upright belting to the heavens . The theatre was electric . <p> Lyricist Dean Bryant and composer Mathew Frank wrote this defining number many years ago . Development of the show came through the Jeanne Pratt artist-in-residence program at Monash University in 2019 , the City of Stonnington and MTC 's Next Stage Writers ' Program . Musicals take a long time to gestate and ongoing support for theatre -- especially musical theatre -- in this country is rare . It 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ find itself . <p> Bryant and Frank have been working together for 25 years , writing musicals and cabaret , among various other endeavours . @@117994720 <h> Haruki Murakami The City and Its Uncertain Walls <p> How does a writer choose their subject matter ? Haruki Murakami tends to give an honest answer . " There are many things I like , " he told The New Yorker in 2019 . " I like wells . I like refrigerators . I like elephants . The filling was feta and mint , and I remember them being absolutely delicious . It came as a great shock to me when , as a young adult then living in the inner city , I bought myself a large filo triangle expecting the taste of my childhood , only to be disappointed by the filling of a regular spanakopita . C. <p> Peel the eggplant and cut into small dice . @@118061215 <h> Book Review : A family legacy explored in Emily Tsokos Purtill 's Matia <p> Emily Tsokos Purtill 's debut novel took her ten years to write . Ten years in which she was also building a promising legal career and a family . It 's no surprise then , that family is at the heart of Matia -- the story of four generations of women from a Greek Australian family . <p> The matia of the title refer to four mati -- or evil eye pendants , worn by the bearer to ward off ill fortune -- given by Sia , the matriarch of the family to her daughter , grand-daughter and great grand-daughter . They symbolise the bond they all share no matter where they are . <p> The novel weaves back and forth in time , and is told from the point of view of the four women in a non-chronological order . There is Sia ( Anastasia ) who arrives in Fremantle in 1945 with her aunt , joining her father who is already in Western Australia working on fishing boats . <p> Before leaving Greece @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ her four prophecies and four matia charms for the women in her family . A choice that Sia makes early on to help another woman sees her trapped in a volatile marriage . But , Sia 's strength and loyalty to the women around her continue throughout her life despite the trouble she might find herself in . <p> Her daughter , Koula , marries the man of her dreams and together they build the family legacy when they start a company that makes Greek yoghurt . Koula 's desperation to hold on to traditional ways and values often puts her at odds with her daughter Athena , who feels more Australian than Greek , but her efforts to be modern do n't always lead to happiness . Athena and her twin children , Clara and Sam , end up in New York . It is Clara , in the portions of the novel set in the world of the future , who will complete the circle and travel to Sia 's home village , just as the four prophecies predicted . <p> While the novel 's timeline is ambitious @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ completely in control as she leads them back and forth through the lives of the four characters . Each woman has a voice distinctly their own , and despite their differences , they are all eminently relatable . Tsokos Purtill is skilled at showing their similarities whilst also showing how they are each a product of their own time and place -- Sia 's adherence to a familial sense of duty , Koula 's feeling of safety within an immigrant community which keeps to the old ways , Athena 's rebellion against tradition and sense of adventure , and finally Clara , who always seems to be a little adrift . <p> Tsokos Purtill writes moments of tension between the generations extremely well , with dialogue that is pitch perfect and could almost have been lifted word for word from eavesdropping on a real family . The scene in which Koula and her husband Evan visit Athena and her partner Richard for lunch is particularly memorable , and wryly funny in a ' if you do n't laugh , you 'll cry ' way . <p> While this is not @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ novel which ask about the world that we are leaving for future generations . Clara 's later sections , for example , look at the impact of climate change on the world with great subtlety . Clara questions the idea of being the end of the line , and the ethics of bringing children into the world -- a question which is , in itself , completely at odds with the ways of her grandmother and great-grandmother . <p> This is a beautiful , heartfelt book about family , love and tradition , and the different ways to be a strong woman . With echoes of Melina Marchetta , this is sure to mark the launch of another promising career for Emily Tsokos Purtill . <h> FIVE STARS ( OUT OF FIVE ) <p> Emily Tsokos Purtill 's Matia is out now through UWA Publishing . @@118065096 <p> From Pacific leaders to regional intelligence analysts , climate change is consistently identified as the foremost security issue for the Pacific island region . Yet Australia 's current defence and intelligence approach to regional engagement , focused mainly on traditional defence , fails to adequately address this existential concern , leaving a gap in its strategy . <p> Greater integration of climate security issues into Australia 's defence and intelligence establishments , drawing inspiration from the United States ' approach , could improve Australia 's Pacific reputation . It would demonstrate that Australia takes the threat of climate change seriously and streamline regional mitigation , adaptation and preparedness efforts . With growing geopolitical competition in the region and the likely US retreat from climate-security leadership , this has never been of greater strategic importance . <p> Australia 's National Defence Strategy is clear that deepening Pacific relationships is key to our strategy of deterrence by denial . We seek to build and maintain these relationships mainly through traditional security arrangements , particularly by delivering what the strategy calls a ' comprehensive package ' of maritime security infrastructure , equipment @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ seem to be greatly enhancing our strategic influence in the Pacific . This should come as no surprise , as the strategy fails to account for the full breadth of security priorities and threat perceptions of its subject countries . <p> Since the early 1990s , Pacific island leaders have made it clear that climate change is their greatest security challenge . As the high commissioner of the Solomon Islands to Australia said in 2020 , ' climate change , not Covid-19 , not even China , is the biggest threat to our security ' -- a threat , and plea for action , that Australia is perceived to have largely ignored . <p> Australia remains one of the largest greenhouse gas emitters per capita . Considering this -- along with sentiments such as Palau President Surangel Whipps Jr 's statement that world leaders who remain inactive on climate issues ' may as well bomb ' Pacific nations -- how can Australia expect to be the Pacific 's partner of choice ? <p> In contrast , the US has been a global leader when it comes to matters of climate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ change ' at the heart ' of its national security . With the recent US Framework for Climate Resilience and Security , the 2022 National Security Strategy and the 2021 National Intelligence Estimate , the US 's defense and intelligence community leads the way in monitoring , analysing and assessing climate security threats . This information is crucial to streamlining mitigation and adaptation policies , identifying priority areas of investment and ensuring adequate preparedness not only domestically , but for partners across the globe . <p> Climate security leadership gave the US a significant and under-recognised advantage in the Pacific : it demonstrated its commitment to , unity with , and genuine respect for the people of the region and advanced the US 's status as the preferred partner . <p> But with an incoming president who has previously called climate change a hoax , US climate security leadership is likely at its end . <p> With China 's domination in almost every aspect of the renewable energy transition likely to win Beijing favour throughout the Pacific , climate security is an emerging gap in the West 's regional strategy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , it must urgently step up and lead in the climate security space . Leaving this area uncontested risks further compromising Australia 's regional influence , ceding the upper hand to other players in the region . <p> Australia 's capacity to engage with matters of climate security is much smaller than that of the US , so identifying and acting upon leverage points will be necessary . Australia should adopt a climate security strategy based on what has been the US strategy -- one that considers how Australia 's National Intelligence Community can best be mobilised to monitor and assess climate security threats . <p> To facilitate this process , Australia should establish a climate intelligence working group . <p> This group should be a partnership between relevant scientific and intelligence agencies , similar to the United States Climate Security Advisory Council . It should identify and advise the government on priority areas of focus , which should be resourced and supported accordingly . Group output may , for example , include an annual net assessment , from which public and partner products could be produced . <p> This @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ intelligence establishments will demonstrate the seriousness with which Australia considers climate security threats . By affirming our commitment to and partnership with Pacific island nations in overcoming these threats , Australia may garner substantial favour throughout the region . <p> Furthermore , Australian leadership in this space would highlight Pacific islanders ' calls for urgent global climate action . As stated by Whipps , ' the hardest challenge , I think , is sometimes you get drowned out -- people denying that it actually is happening .... ' <p> Australia can ensure that our neighbours ' voices are amplified , not drowned out . <p> If we want to persist with our current strategy , rather than adopt one that relies less on our Pacific partners , it 's time to take climate security seriously . <p> As former Samoan prime minister Tuila'epa Sa'ilele Malielegaoi said , ' We all know the problem , the solutions . All that is left would be some courage to tell people there is certainty of disaster . ' 
@@118065101 <p> Senate estimates earlier this month heard the remarkable revelation that Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has had to take ' precautions ' based on warnings from his own department to protect himself and the nation 's sensitive information from Burke 's own Chinese-made electric car . <p> The risks with such cars , according to Home Affairs officials , might include having data collected from the owner 's phone if it were connected to the car , voice calls eavesdropped on , image collection from the car 's external cameras and geolocation tracking -- meaning that if Burke drove to a sensitive government location the car 's manufacturer would be able to see . <p> The United States has announced plans to ban Chinese technology in American cars over surveillance and sabotage concerns . Australia should do the same . Moreover , with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese meeting China 's President Xi Jinping in Brazil on the sidelines of the G20 meeting overnight , he had the chance to raise this issue directly , consistent with the kind of frank diplomatic engagement for which Australia should be using these @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ strategy to address the rolling security threat of high-risk foreign vendors to critical infrastructure . Our current approach -- not addressing risks until Chinese firms dominate their markets , as BYD is doing now in electric cars -- is woefully inadequate . We are trapped in a game of whac-a-mole . <p> Australia has previously addressed risks from China 's Huawei , TikTok and camera-maker Hikvision . New technologies will keep coming , bringing risks of malicious use by Beijing . <p> Australia must see the US ban on Chinese tech in cars not as an escalation in the US -- China trade war but as a wakeup call : technological advance is core to strategic competition and presents real security threats that need to be confronted . <p> China 's technological dominance across hardware and software allows smart cars , for instance , to serve as tools for surveillance , propaganda and sabotage . But this is n't just about cars . Internet-connected medical devices , for example , can be used for surveillance of patients . <p> Most countries could not interfere with and hack into foreign technology @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ technology that Beijing -- and its intelligence agencies -- could exploit directly . <p> Just this year , seven Chinese departments , including the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology , called for innovation and industrial development in such areas as 6G communications , satellite internet and direct satellite-to-mobile connectivity . This is to be done by advancing current technology that is already raising foreign concerns : 5G , internet of things , satellite communications and internet-connected vehicles . <p> This aggressive push for leadership highlights the risk of continuing to rely on technology from a country that seeks to do us harm -- a country that is using a military-civil fusion strategy to ensure all of its society works for the regime 's military ambitions . <p> Australia needs a strategic framework that moves beyond a whac-a-mole approach that will fail in a plague of moles . Ideally this would involve a coalition of like-minded democratic partners taking collective action . But in the meantime , Australia must develop its own framework . <p> We need a policy that lists critical infrastructure and sectors from which suppliers of concern @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Excluding those suppliers would be based on the scale of the potential threat and our inability to mitigate that threat . <p> This would provide certainty and avoid having to manage fallout from imposing bans after the suppliers were already in the market . Government agencies could still assess specific cases for mitigation . But the presumption that high-risk vendors are banned would end the current approach of waiting for them to achieve a potentially harmful position before we act , as with TikTok . <p> Australia 's ban on Chinese suppliers in the 5G network in 2018 proved the value of this approach . Australia considered carefully whether the risk of Chinese suppliers in its 5G network could be mitigated . A vendor 's control of the 5G network gives it the capability to turn the network off . Even if China had no immediate plan to take such a dramatic step , its objectives could quickly change in any future conflict or crisis . Australia therefore made the assessment that a full ban was the only option . <p> While awaiting a national strategy , the same principle @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ there was a distinction between 4G and 5G networks , there should be a distinction between traditional , unconnected cars and the new , connected ones . If Chinese technology is too dangerous for our critical infrastructure but not for cars that connect with that critical infrastructure , the government should explain why . <p> TikTok was deemed a national security threat , but Australia did not ban it outright , opting instead to ban it from government devices . If an outright 5G-style ban on cars is assessed as unnecessary , surely consistency means prohibiting government employees and politicians from buying or travelling in those with Chinese technology . After all , these cars would connect to the devices , such as phones , that the government has said must not be linked to untrusted technology . Choice can not be the principle upon which security decisions are made . Nor can price . <p> Australia needs @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Chinese tech ca n't be in the 5G network , nor in government devices , but can be in the cars that connect to both . <p> Author <p> Justin Bassi is executive director and Tilla Hoja is a China analyst at ASPI . @@118065157 <h> European EV battery hopes fade after Northvolt files for bankruptcy protection in US <p> Swedish battery developer and manufacturer Northvolt has filed for bankruptcy protection in the United States , in a move that was followed a day later by the resignation of the company 's founder CEO , former senior Tesla executive Peter Carlsson . <p> It 's a significant move because Northvolt was one of the brightest hopes for Western electric carmakers that were looking to reduce their reliance on China battery giants . The company raised more than $10 billion , but was unable to land long term contracts with major car makers or compete with Chinese competitors . <p> Northvolt makes a range of battery products including lithium-ion and sodium-ion cells , electric vehicle ( EV ) battery cells , and batteries for standalone storage . Last year it hailed a breakthrough in sodium-ion batteries , which the company said would enable the expansion of cost-efficient and sustainable energy storage systems around the globe . <p> Its filing for Chapter 11 is designed to facilitate approximately $US145 million in cash collateral and a further $US100 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ $US100 million promised late last week by Swedish truck maker Scania , a shareholder and Northvolt 's biggest customer . <p> Tom Johnstone , the interim chairman of the board , said the company is not giving up on its hopes to play a key role in the transition to electric vehicles . <p> " Despite near-term challenges , this action to strengthen our capital structure will allow us to capture the continued market demand for vehicle electrification , " he said in a statement . " We are likewise pleased by the strong support we have received from our existing lenders and our customers . " <p> Northvolt , with operations in California , reportedly has only $US30 million in cash , enough only to support operations for around a week . The company also has debts worth $US5.8 billion . <p> Carlsson , who was a former Tesla executive and co-founded Northvolt in 2016 , will stay on as a member of the board and senior advisor . <p> Joshua S. " <p> Additionally , these issues can often be addressed through efforts in a company 's everyday operations and the composition of its board and management teams , leading them to be perceived as " more tangible " , he pointed out . <p> " People can see and change this much more immediately . @@118136971 <h> Renewables are exceeding expectations -- but so are emissions . Why ? <p> It is bad enough that 2024 was a record high for global greenhouse gas emissions . It is extra bad because the number we 've ended up at is higher than all of the old projections of what this year would end up at . That is to say : we are underestimating our ability to stop using fossil fuels . <p> There have been incredible advances in renewables and climate policies , but also , " fossil fuel subsidies remain at an all-time high and funding for fossil fuel-prolonging projects quadrupled between 2021 and 2022 " . Why ? What is justifying this weird refusal to back away from the fossil fuel economy ? <p> It 's many things , but a big one is the false promise of a machine that cleans up fossil fuels , rather than us needing to find a replacement for them . <p> Back in 2022 , I contributed an essay to Greta Thunberg 's Climate Book . It was about the weaponised false promise of carbon capture and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it not as a technological phenomenon but a rhetorical one . A tactically deployed promise that is never meant to come true . Failure as a feature , not a bug . <h> The second coming has n't come yet <p> After a surge of planned projects in the late 2000s and early 2010s failed to turn into operational carbon capture sites , there was a lull . But since 2020 , the volume of planned CCS has increased very significantly , as we can see from the latest update from the Global CCS Institute ( GCCSi ) , a CCS reporting and advocacy group that publishes annual data : <p> As with so many previous years , the change in " operational " CCS is small . The pipeline for CCS has been surging for a half-decade now , and the amount of operational CCS has only grown by a few megatonnes of capacity . We were promised a CCS revolution , and we are n't getting one . <p> Each year 's database puts an estimated " start date " on these CCS projects , so if we @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ an idea of what should be operational , and compare it to what is : <p> In 2024 , the amount of operational CCS should be several times higher than it actually is , based on the promised start dates of projects in older reports . Some projects are being cancelled , others are pushing out those dates further into the future due to frequentdelays . Carbon capture is n't a technology that likes to be built . <p> It 's almost a cruel chart to make , but compare the percentage growth in operational CCS to the growth in wind and solar over the same time , and you get an idea of the different dynamics we 're dealing with here : <p> Why do we keep believing the promise when it keeps failing to materialise ? There are many reasons , but I want to dive into a specific one in this post : a range of different future scenarios , from a range of different sources , has leant hard on CCS as a way to minimise projected reductions in fossil fuel use , and therefore politically @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ elimination of fossil fuels . <h> What the future looks like <p> Fossil fuel companies ( both power generation and extractive ) love using the false promise of CCS to justify massive , high-emitting projects . It 's worth diving into this incredible July 2024 investigation by Drilled 's Amy Westervelt , specifically on how fossil fuel companies were actively aware that their promises on CCS were hollow . <p> Using the data made available in the latest Global Energy Outlook , I 've made a little illustration of how fossil fuel companies use assumptions about CCS in their scenarios that are weirdly disconnected from the material realities of ultra-slow deployment : <p> Equinor , my friendly local state-owned fossil fuel company , are comfortably the worst offender here . In 2022 , 2023 and 2024 , the 2030 assumptions for CCS are deeply bonkers and far exceed Shell and British Petroleum 's assumptions . This is despite Equinor being notably off track even for their own company CCS targets . <p> I 've created a compilation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " net-zero " scenario , and you can immediately see that as far as CCS is from even realising its own pipeline of planned projects , the gap between the assumptions in the IEA 's net-zero scenario is significantly worse : <p> If CCS development were truly following the IEA 's 2022 net-zero scenario , operational capacity today would be about 12 times what it ended up being this year . The IEA 's 2024 scenario , released a few weeks ago , assumes that CCS capacity will be around 25 times greater in 2030 than it is today . <p> CCUS deployment tripled over the last decade , albeit from a low base -- but it has fallen well short of expectations . In 2009 , the IEA roadmap for CCUS set a target of developing 100 large-scale CCUS projects between 2010 and 2020 to meet global climate goals , storing around 300 MtCO2 per year . Actual capacity is only around 40 Mt -- just 13% of the target . <p> The IEA 's net-zero scenario was a big deal , when they first gave it a go @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the first scenario the group published that started with a temperature goal , and then solved backwards . But to solve that equation , it has consistently relied on a volume of CCS deployment that does n't seem to be matched by real-world manifestation -- and models need to change to reflect the persistent reality . <p> To continue the comparison with wind and solar , these two technologies exhibit the exact opposite effect : the IEA 's scenarios have historically underestimated the deployment of the technologies ( across all their scenarios ) . It said as much in its 2023 " oil and gas transitions " report , where it pointed out CCS in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ produced would require " 26,000 terawatt hours of electricity generation to operate in 2050 , which is more than global electricity demand in 2022 " , and would also require " over US$3.5 trillion in annual investments all the way from today through to mid-century , which is an amount equal to the entire industry 's annual average revenue in recent years " . <p> The IEA has also been at pains to point out it is not the worst offender when it comes to leaning on CCS to model climate ambition , showing that its reliance on CCS in net-zero models is a lot lower than the IPCC 's reliance on CCS . It 's not wrong . <p> A recent study by Tsimafei Kazlou , Aleh Cherp and Jessica Jewell published in Nature showed that if you consider a reasonable but optimistic feasibility of CCS growth , that is still significantly slower than what 90% of IPCC 1.5c mitigation pathways assume ( noting that the recent AR6 report does go to some lengths to include some CCS-free scenarios ) . @@118153097 <h> Black Friday Is Rubbish <p> As Black Friday approaches , Mike Smith , founder of Zero Co shares the devastating impact of overconsumption on our planet and offers tips to adopt a more sustainable approach to generating profit and buying products . <p> As the founder of Zero Co and someone who has spent the past four years cleaning some of the world 's dirtiest oceans , rivers , and beaches , I 've witnessed firsthand the devastating impact of overconsumption on our planet . <p> While I understand the necessity for businesses to generate profit , it 's imperative that we transition to a more sustainable version of capitalism -- one that balances people , planet , and profit . Black Friday and Cyber Monday epitomise unsustainable consumption , and their environmental impact is staggering . <h> The Environmental Toll of Black Friday and Cyber Monday <p> Black Friday and Cyber Monday have become global phenomena , driving a frenzy of consumerism with promises of unbeatable deals . However , beneath the allure of discounts lies a hidden cost : significant damage to our environment . From increased @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ events exacerbate environmental challenges at a time when sustainable living has never been more critical . <h> Carbon Footprint of Black Friday <p> The transportation of goods purchased during Black Friday and Cyber Monday significantly contributes to greenhouse gas emissions . Deliveries from Black Friday sales in the UK alone are estimated to generate over 429,000 metric tons of CO2 , equivalent to the emissions from 435 return flights between London and New York . Globally , the numbers are even more alarming , adding significantly to our collective carbon footprint . <p> Transitioning to sustainable development and renewable energy in logistics is crucial to mitigating these impacts . However , these changes require systemic efforts from businesses and consumers alike to prioritize green technology and energy efficiency over short-term gains . <h> Waste and Plastic Pollution <p> The waste generated during Black Friday and Cyber Monday is equally concerning . It 's estimated that 80 per cent of items purchased , along with their packaging , are discarded after just a few uses . Much of this waste ends up in landfills or , worse , pollutes natural ecosystems @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Most products come encased in layers of plastic , contributing to the 141 million tonnes of plastic packaging produced globally each year . @@118195875 <p> With record-breaking spring heat sapping Sydney , it seems like the perfect time for a southerly buster to sweep over the city . But Speer does n't expect one on Thursday , with stormy weather blowing in from the northwest instead . <p> For a southerly buster to be declared , gusts blowing north must exceed 54 kilometres per hour , or 15 metres per second , and the temperature must drop by at least 5 degrees over three hours , according to the Bureau of Meteorology . <p> Since the 1970s , it has n't been unusual for Sydney to experience between two and five annual " severe " busters , which can slash temperatures by 20 degrees within an hour and summon winds of at least 74 km/h . <p> These powerful blasts dominated Sydney until 1995 , when weaker busters below 74 km/h became more common , according to a recent paper published by Speer and his colleagues . @@118197550 <h> The problem with networks : Where to put batteries -- and EV chargers -- on the grid <p> The integration of CER seems to come down to three key things : ( i ) everyone having a modern meter , ( ii ) working out who loses when there is too much solar and minimising that loss through storage and ( iii ) working out whether we really want lots of household storage including EV related storage . <p> And if we do want those things , how is the network to be equitably funded ? <p> What 's also clear to me is that for so long as networks are regulated monopolies , they can be safely ignored by everyone except the Australian Energy Regulator . Pilots will make their customary announcement to begin the phase , usually at cruising altitudes above 30,000 feet . That means that cabin crew begin preparing the aircraft for landing before securing themselves in their jump seats . <h> What Forced the Change ? <p> Flight attendant safety is the main motivation here . Turbulence is one of the biggest causes of injuries to cabin crew , and turbulence -- though possible at any elevation -- is much more likely to occur at lower altitudes thanks to thicker clouds and more changeable weather patterns . That means that landing is primetime for these injuries , and by getting flight attendants seated sooner , the risk of their getting injured during landing should be significantly reduced . <p> " The change in procedures is designed to reduce the risk of in-flight turbulence injuries for our Crew Members and Customers . It is the result of the airline 's close collaboration with its Labor Partners and a robust approach to Safety Management . Previously , preparation for landing began at 10,000 feet . @@118239210 <p> Researchers in the U.S. and Austria have created the first world map highlighting regions repeatedly experiencing intense heat waves that greatly exceed global warming models . The map , detailed in a November 26 study published in PNAS , shows these unexplainable hotspots residing on every continent , save for Antarctica . Alarmingly , the associated heat waves have killed tens of thousands of people and destroyed environments by causing droughts and wildfires , according to a Columbia Climate School statement . <p> " This is about extreme trends that are the outcome of physical interactions we might not completely understand , " Kai Kornhuber of the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis in Austria and lead writer on the study said in the statement . " These regions become temporary hothouses . " Kornhuber is also an adjunct scientist at the Columbia Climate School 's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory . <p> The Columbia-led team focused on unexpected heat waves over the past 65 years , though most occurred in the last half a decade . This approach identified regions where the temperature increase is accelerating quickly and has repeatedly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , in 2021 , a nine-day heatwave in the U.S. Pacific Northwest and southwestern Canada broke some local daily records by 54 degrees Fahrenheit ( 30 degrees Celsius ) . <p> More broadly , the map marks hotspots in central China , Japan , Korea , the Arabian peninsula , eastern Australia , parts of Africa , Canada 's Northwest Territories and its High Arctic islands , northern Greenland , the southern end of South America , and parts of Siberia , with the most extreme and consistent in northwestern Europe , where fewer people have air conditioning than in the United States . <p> " The large and unexpected margins by which recent regional-scale extremes have broken earlier records have raised questions about the degree to which climate models can provide adequate estimates of relations between global mean temperature changes and regional climate risks , " the researchers wrote in the study . In other words , the rising average global temperature might not reflect the extreme heat reality of certain local climates in the way that models predicted . <p> What makes the phenomenon even stranger is that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of north-central United States , south-central Canada , and South America , as well as much of Siberia , northern Africa , and northern Australia also have rising temperatures , their peaks are lower than those forecast by models . <p> Scientists do n't know what 's causing this disparity . A previous study led by Kornhuber hypothesized that changes in the northern jet stream ( strong winds that circle the Earth from west to east ) were to blame for the hotspots in Europe and Russia , but the theory does n't explain all the extremes , according to the new research . Another 2021 study led by Columbia University graduate student Samuel Bartusek , who is also a co-author of the new study , also suggested factors behind the 2021 Pacific Northwest/southwestern Canada heat wave , including similar disruptions to the jet streams , drying vegetation without water reserves to evaporate , and atmospheric events that brought heat from the Pacific Ocean surface to land . <p> " Due to their unprecedented nature , these heat waves are usually linked to very severe health impacts , and can @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Kornhuber concluded in the statement . " We 're not built for them , and we might not be able to adapt fast enough . " <p> Though the United States is better equipped than other countries to handle spiking temperatures , heat nevertheless takes the lives of more people in the U.S. each year than any other extreme weather event . With COP29 having just come to a close , it remains to be seen how nations will act to mitigate the impact of climate change on the world 's most vulnerable communities .

@@118263136 <h> Spotlight on Sustainability Award winner Holocene House by CPlusC <p> Holocene House , designed by CplusC Architects + Builders , is a pioneering example of regenerative residential architecture located in Manly , Sydney . <p> Completed in 2023 , it became the first home in Australia to receive certification from the international Active House Alliance , reflecting its exceptional balance between occupant comfort and environmental performance . <p> Recipient of the prestigious Single Dwelling ( New ) award at the Sustainability Awards 2024 , the jury described Holocene House as " an adventure to move through " . <p> The team sits down with Architecture &amp; Design 's Digital Editor Cl ? mence Carayol to discuss their victory for this exceptional project . <p> Architecture &amp; Design : Why do you think you were honoured for your entry ? <p> CplusC Architects + Builders : It is important to not only support all our peers and the work they do in this critically important part of our industry . Those pushing the boundaries of sustainable architecture and design are the true leaders of our industry , paving the way @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a common goal , we all have unique businesses and individual client needs which create unique project outcomes , albeit , with a common foundation . In this regard , it is important that the sustainability certification we choose for our projects are aligned with the values and assessment criteria suitable to our projects and clients ' values . <p> In our case the Active House Alliance certification system was most suited to this project and clients ' requirements to deliver a project that worked with the Sydney climate with a highly sustainable , thermally comfortable and energy efficient home . We are fortunate to have clients that wanted to push the boundary of what 's possible in terms of regeneration and show that sustainability is not enough as we the face the challenges of climate change . <p> The Holocene House was awarded the first Active House Alliance certification in Australia . " It said the highest inflation in decades was being driven by " an explosion of profits " as companies exploited supply disruptions to maximise their returns . <p> Weber drew a parallel between the pandemic period and the end of World War II . In both circumstances , a release of pent-up demand coincided with supply bottlenecks . They now face a similar choice , Weber argued : impose strategic price controls or tolerate the profits explosion driving inflation . <p> The response was brutal : Weber was scorned , her argument ridiculed , and not just by Fox @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , a columnist for The New York Times and darling of the liberal intelligentsia , called her " truly stupid " . <p> Then Russia invaded Ukraine . The European Union regulated gas prices , the US regulated oil prices , the G7 nations began enforcing a global cap on the price of petroleum products from Russia . @@118278047 <h> Jennifer Robinson The trial of Hong Kong democracy activist Jimmy Lai <p> The world watched as Jimmy Lai , Hong Kong 's oldest and most prominent political prisoner , finally took the stand last week to give evidence in his trial under the controversial and far-reaching National Security Law ( NSL ) . This pivotal moment unfolded less than 24 hours after harsh sentences , ranging from four years and two months to 10 years in prison , were handed down to 45 other pro-democracy activists , including an Australian citizen , Gordon Ng . Such heavy-handed punishments underscore the law 's true purpose and its intended result : to silence dissent , instil fear and destroy democracy . <p> Jimmy Lai is my client -- a 77-year-old British citizen in increasingly ill health , who faces the very real prospect of spending the rest of his life behind bars . He has spent nearly four years in solitary confinement . The United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention has found that his detention is arbitrary and unlawful and has called for his immediate release . The United Kingdom @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the world and in Australia have also called for his release . But Mr Lai remains in prison -- and his ongoing trial and its outcome serve as a litmus test on the rapid erosion of human rights , press freedom , democracy and the rule of law in Hong Kong . <p> The enactment of the NSL in 2020 marked a turning point in Hong Kong 's political landscape . Ostensibly aimed at safeguarding national security , the law 's sweeping provisions were immediately used to stifle free speech and punish peaceful protest . <p> This erosion of freedoms is not just a violation of the rights of Hong Kong 's citizens but a betrayal of the commitments made during the 1997 handover of Hong Kong from the UK to China . Beijing promised to preserve Hong Kong 's autonomy under the " one country , two systems " framework , ensuring protections for democratic rights and freedoms -- and the rights protected under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights ( ICCPR ) . Those promises are now worthless . <p> Mr Lai is currently on trial @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . His alleged crimes include commissioning opinion pieces , engaging in peaceful advocacy and meeting with foreign politicians to discuss human rights violations . These activities , which should be celebrated in any free society , have instead been labelled crimes and threats to national security . <p> Australians need to be aware of the risks posed by this law , which claims jurisdiction over anyone , anywhere , who engages in activities deemed threatening to Hong Kong 's national security . As senators warned ... this threatens the exercise of internationally protected rights in Australia . <p> Mr Lai 's story is inspiring . These values are now being systematically dismantled -- with the case against Mr Lai becoming emblematic of the broader struggle for democracy and freedom in Hong Kong . <p> Through Apple Daily and his own writing , Mr Lai was an outspoken critic of the Beijing and Hong Kong authorities . By Philippa Hawker . <h> Archivist Peter Steinberg 's 30 years of devotion to Sylvia Plath <p> Peter Steinberg was told that everyone goes through a Sylvia Plath phase . " Mine , " he says , " has lasted 30 years . " But after the publication on December 3 of The Collected Prose of Sylvia Plath -- the culmination of years of archival research and editing -- he is finally moving on . <p> Steinberg evolved from avid reader to Plath blogger to the author of two books about her to the co-editor of two volumes of her letters . At 846 pages , TheCollected Prose of Sylvia Plath is the culmination of his work , embracing everything from juvenilia to college journalism to short stories to book reviews to fiction fragments . <p> He remembers exactly where his obsession started . In 1995 , in his first year of college in Virginia , a poetry @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ after a break-up with a girlfriend . It is a scorching , complex poem , fierce and ironic , but there was something about its assertion of survival and renewal that he found helpful . It sparked an immediate fascination . He went on to seek out more of Plath 's work , despite little encouragement from his teachers . <p> Plath might be one of the best known and most influential of 20th century poets , a staple of school and university curriculums with an impact across popular culture and literature alike . But she has also endured widespread , dismissive verdicts from those who regard her as the object of an adolescent female cult , a literary celebrity or a self-absorbed self-mythologiser . <p> For Steinberg , none of this mattered . " At that point my aim was to consume everything I could over the next couple of years , go to used bookstores to find what I did n't have , " he says . He read her novel , The Bell Jar , in December 1995 ( and has read it every June and December @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ she was so professional at such an early age , and so resilient , dealing with so many rejections , because she would not take no for an answer . " <p> Three years later , he made his first visit to an archive at Smith College in Massachusetts , Plath 's alma mater , where she also taught briefly . It has an extensive holding of Plath material : manuscripts , drafts , letters , correspondence , books from her own library , personal items of every kind , including her typewriter and , in a separate collection , her prom dress . <p> There was , he says , an immediate feeling of recognition . " I was blown away . It was archive at first sight . " He thought he had read most of her work but discovered otherwise . " I was so new to Plath and that world , I did n't realise how much material was n't published and was n't readily available . It reveals how Plath experimented with popular modes , trying out everything from the gothic to the sentimental , how she explored genre , tone and varieties of female experience . It also illuminates other aspects of her work . You can see , for example , how she used the experience of fruit-picking as material for every kind of writing . " It goes from short fiction , into journalism , even into poetry , several different styles of writing over a three- or four-year period or more , " Steinberg says . " It 's something she routinely went back to when she needed some inspiration or in the case of the poem ' Memoirs of a Spinach-Picker ' a quick 10 bucks from TheChristian Science Monitor . " <p> In her college years , Plath kept meticulous records of work she submitted to magazines , with columns @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ was something she honed early on , " Steinberg says . " I find it inspirational that she was so professional at such an early age , and so resilient , dealing with so many rejections , because she would not take no for an answer . " <p> The Plath canon and the Plath story have expanded and transformed since her death by suicide in 1963 at the age of 30 . The history of her posthumous publication and reputation is complicated and contested . She had work published from her teens , and established herself within literary circles , first in the United States , where she was born and grew up , and in England , where she spent the last years of her life . <p> Yet before her death she had published only one book under her own name , a 1960 poetry collection titled The Colossus and other poems . The Bell Jar , her novel , had just appeared in Britain , published under a pseudonym . She did not leave a will and her literary estate became the property of her estranged @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ poetry collection , Ariel , ready to submit to publishers . She knew what she was achieving in this work , telling her mother in a letter , " I am writing the best poems of my life . They will make my name . " <p> When Ariel eventually came out in 1965 , it was edited by Hughes . The order was rearranged and some poems were removed , others added . By then , the fascination with Plath had grown apace , and so had controversy about the way her work was being presented . First Hughes , then his sister , Olwyn , handled the Plath estate , dealing with the publication of her work and responding to increasing interest from biographers , critics and academics . The estate was often charged with being defensive and controlling , hostile in particular to feminist analysis of Plath and quick to withdraw cooperation . <p> For Steinberg , this approach was self-sabotaging . " The Hugheses had obvious intentions about how Plath was going to be presented to the world , but they botched it so badly that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " he says . " Plath would always have been interesting , she would always have been well known , but if they had been more forthcoming from the beginning , the way that the reading public understood her would have been far different . Coleman . <h> Bagan bariwariganyan : echoes of country a once-in-a-lifetime experience <p> The gunyah ( shelter ) is the bagan bariwariganyan 's biggest installation . <p> Every trip to Bundanon art museum is an adventure . If you share this taste with me , or are simply curious , it 's a good @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Wiradjuri and Kamilaroi artist Jonathan Jones works in site-specific art , mostly installations that draw on the stories and the landscape of the places where he is working , understanding the location in which the art will reside and often critiquing it . Bundanon gallery is on land once owned by Arthur Boyd , and was before that , obviously , Aboriginal land . It 's a custom-built gallery in what looks a bit like a bunker -- rectangular , boxy , white-walled and concrete -- half-buried to integrate seamlessly with the landscape . Inside it 's a classic " white cube " gallery , only differentiated from some other galleries by the near complete lack of windows to the outside world , which has the side effect of offering more hanging space for art . <p> Bagan bariwariganyan consists of three immersive installations , each filling one of the three rooms , each telling a story and each with its own soundscapes . <p> As Jonathan said : " The only way that you can engage with a site is with local Elders , local people who @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ know the history , know the stories . @@118278054 <h> Chicken baked in bread <p> I have tried several times to cook turkey for a Christmas-time celebration but , while stopping short of saying it is n't possible to deliver a delicious one , I do wonder , why bother ? Made larger by bread dough . <p> When roasting a chicken , bread is more often found on the inside in the form of stuffing , which has the benefit of capturing the juice from the cavity . However , in cooking the chicken inside a bread crust , you can kind of have your cake and eat it too . There 's a crispy " skin " and the entire loaf tastes like chicken . <p> My view may be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ anyway . Whether it 's as confronting as cooking in an animal 's stomach or simply wrapping vegetables in a greaseproof paper parcel , the idea is to use the moisture from the food to steam itself . Do a little research into the cooking method en papillote , French for " in paper " , to find myriad preparation suggestions . <p> When cooking in bread I find smaller poultry gets the best results . The contents must also be on the bone or in whole form , as much as possible . For a whole chicken , you will need to cook it for longer than one hour , which means the bread is largely sacrificed in order to cook the meat or interior enough . Place the mixture @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ leave in the fridge overnight . <p> The next morning pull the dough out and allow it to come to room temperature ( about 30 minutes ) , then put a " turn " into the dough . Pick up one edge , stretch it up and then fold it into the centre of the dough , then turn 90 degrees and repeat , all the way around . This helps build and strengthen the bread . Place the bowl back in the fridge and repeat the " turns " twice more through the day . <p> Pull the dough out of the fridge around lunchtime , then leave it at room temperature to double in size for its final proof . Tip it out onto a work surface and place the chicken on top . Season the chicken well with salt and pepper and lay the bay leaves on top along with any other flavour you want in there , such as garlic or thyme . Pull the bread dough around the chicken and then seal it at the top . <p> Pick the whole thing up and transfer @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ oven at 180 ? C for 80 minutes . <p> Remove from oven and let the loaf sit for 20 minutes . Do n't be tempted to peek inside -- the cooking process is still happening and will continue for quite some time if the crust is n't broken . For a precise result you could use a temperature probe , but be sure not to create too big a hole from which steam can escape . <p> Cut the top off the bread crust and pull it away until it reveals the chicken . Lift the chicken out and carve it onto a plate to be shared . There was the form of the tourists , recently thrashed 3-0 at home by New Zealand , and the talismanic Virat Kohli , who is these days breathing the air of mortals -- once the world 's best batsman , he 'd scored only two centuries in the past half decade . <p> India were also without five of their best , including their captain Rohit Sharma and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ wicketkeeper and swashbuckler , Rishabh Pant , had only recently returned to Test cricket after having a knee remade after a near-fatal car crash in late 2022 . Here was a transitional squad -- ageing superstars at one end and a cluster of youth at the other . For the First Test , India played two debutants . <p> And sure enough , in the first two sessions of the match , things were happily obliging the script . Having won the toss , stand-in captain Jasprit Bumrah chose to bat and within 30 overs India were 5-59 . Veteran quicks Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc were especially good , the former conceding little with his unerring accuracy , while Starc -- who often mixes menace with errancy -- was almost as consistent . <p> It was a bowling clinic , aided by a lively pitch , all glossy green , its grass cover helping to preserve the ball 's shine . Within just 50 overs , India were bowled out for 150 -- perhaps 30 runs more than they should have been allowed . But after this moment , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of the great pleasures of international cricket is watching Jasprit Bumrah bowl . A man with a curiously modest run-up -- I 've previously described it as like a man trundling to the bar -- he generates intense power from a javelin action and a lightning whipcrack of his wrist . He was unplayable in Australia 's first innings , the discrepancy between his skill and the haplessness of the batters almost comical . <p> Which brings us to Marnus Labuschagne , not long ago an elite batsman but now suffering not so much a form slump as a period of disastrous neuroticism . In Australia 's first innings , the No. ? 3 somehow lasted 52 deliveries -- for just two runs -- while resembling an old man fighting off a swarm of bees with a rolled-up newspaper . <p> As the sun blazed and the Indians patiently accrued their giant lead , the Aussies seemed afflicted by a terrible inertia . There was little banter , few shared affirmations . There was slovenliness in the field and the bowling was unimaginative and increasingly tired . <p> For a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ see the ball -- he moved around the crease with the ease of a self-conscious man forced to join a wedding party 's conga line . Australia were bowled out for 104 . <p> India 's second innings is where the Australian fan may have felt the whiplash of their expectation , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ depressed resignation . On a pitch that had lost its green cover and yet had resisted much visible cracking , the Indian batters were unrecognisable . He left his family home and moved to Mumbai in pursuit of greater sporting opportunity when he was only 12 , and hustled on the streets to make money while he played pick-up games on local ovals . Last weekend , he scored 161 in the second innings , his fourth century in just 15 Tests . <p> As the sun blazed and the Indians patiently accrued their giant lead , the Aussies seemed afflicted by a terrible inertia . After five eccentric and fairly expensive overs , he reverted to his original leg spin -- and a tedious tactic of bowling wide down leg side . It was shabby stuff from a country that prides itself on maintaining positivity , a negative strategy that complemented the surrender suggested by their body language .
